nameStory: The Common Schendyla gets its name from Carl Ludwig Koch, the German scientist who first described it in 1836, though the genus name 'Schendyla' itself comes from an earlier Greek root. It's called 'common' because it's one of the more widespread species in its family, though you'd hardly call any soil centipede truly common since they spend their lives hidden underground. The species name 'nemorensis' means 'of the woods,' hinting at its forest floor preferences.
description: The Common Schendyla is a slender, thread-like centipede that belongs to the soil centipede group called geophilomorphs. Unlike the flattened house centipedes you might see scurrying across your basement floor, this species looks more like a pale, segmented earthworm with tiny legs. It's typically yellowish to light brown in color and moves through soil with a snake-like undulating motion. These centipedes are quite small, usually measuring less than an inch long, making them easy to overlook even when you do encounter them.

idTips.label: Body shape and movement
idTips.description: Long, thin, and worm-like with a smooth, almost silky texture when gently touched - moves with flowing, serpentine waves rather than the quick scuttling of other centipedes

idTips.label: Color and appearance
idTips.description: Pale yellowish-brown to light tan coloration that may appear almost translucent in bright light, giving it an otherworldly, ghostly appearance

idTips.label: Leg count and size
idTips.description: Many pairs of tiny, barely visible legs (usually 30+ pairs) that feel like soft bristles if you let one crawl across your palm

idTips.label: Head and antennae
idTips.description: Small, rounded head that's not much wider than the body, with thread-like antennae that are often the first thing you notice poking out from under leaf litter

idTips.label: Size and segmentation
idTips.description: Less than an inch long with clearly visible body segments that compress and extend like an accordion as it moves through soil

habitat: Look for Common Schendyla in moist, rich forest soils throughout New England's deciduous and mixed woodlands. They prefer areas with thick leaf litter and decaying organic matter, especially under fallen logs, in compost piles, or in the dark spaces between rocks where the soil stays consistently damp. You're most likely to find them in lower elevation forests with maple, oak, and birch trees where the soil has that sweet, earthy smell of active decomposition.

seasonality.spring: Most active as soil warms and becomes workable again - look under newly fallen logs or stones where winter moisture remains. They may appear sluggish as they emerge from deeper soil layers.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're easiest to find by carefully digging through moist leaf litter or compost. Hot, dry periods may drive them deeper underground where they're harder to locate.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to deeper soil layers as temperatures drop. Fresh leaf fall provides new hunting grounds before they settle in for winter.
seasonality.winter: Largely inactive and found deep in soil below the frost line. Occasionally discovered in protected spots like root cellars or unheated basements where soil doesn't freeze.

funFact: Despite having dozens of legs, soil centipedes like the Common Schendyla never trip over themselves because they move their legs in perfectly coordinated waves that flow from front to back - like a living conveyor belt that can instantly reverse direction without missing a step.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with small earthworms, but remember the simple rhyme: 'worms are smooth, centipedes have feet' - even tiny ones you can feel if you let it crawl on your skin. Young millipedes are also similar, but they curl up when disturbed while centipedes keep moving in their characteristic snake-like way.
contextualKnowledge: The word 'centipede' literally means 'hundred feet,' but no centipede actually has exactly 100 legs - they always have an odd number of leg pairs, so the total is never 100. Soil centipedes like Schendyla are often overlooked in nature education because they're less dramatic than house centipedes, but they're actually far more common and important to forest ecosystems.
compareHints: With no other Schendyla species confirmed in New England, compare it to other soil centipedes in the family Schendylidae by looking at size and color - Common Schendyla tends to be lighter colored and smaller than most of its relatives. It's more delicate-looking than the robust Geophilus centipedes and lacks the distinctly darker head coloration seen in some related species.
